name: memex-protocol
description: The canonical protocol for AI tools using memex. Every memex-aware AI session must follow this pattern.

metadata.approach: Memex is your persistent memory and validation layer. (1) Before generating code, RECALL relevant context: `recall("<topic>")`. (2) Before generating code in a sensitive domain (security, money, concurrency, crypto, SQL, user input), VALIDATE the relevant approach: `validate("<approach-name>")`. Self-attest each check it returns; refuse to generate code if a check cannot be satisfied. (3) When you make a non-trivial decision (architecture choice, design tradeoff, library pick), OBSERVE it: `observe(kind="decision", payload={...})`. (4) When you discover a new pattern, constraint, or fact about the project, SAVE it: `add(name=..., description=..., kind=...)`. (5) Periodically check PROGRESS to know what you've already validated: `progress()`. Memex auto-tracks every validation as an episodic event so you never repeat work.
checks: recall() called at least once before generating code in a non-trivial context
validate(<approach>) called for every domain matched by the approach's triggers (security, money, concurrency, crypto, SQL, user input)
the AI has self-attested each check returned by validate() before proceeding
observe() called for any non-trivial decision the AI makes
add() called when a new pattern, constraint, or fact is discovered that future sessions should know
examples_good:
# Start of session
ctx = recall('current auth flow')
# Before generating subprocess code
v = validate('secure-subprocess')
assert all_checks_pass(v['checks'], my_code)
# After deciding
observe(kind='decision', payload={'choice': 'use Reach over WireGuard', 'reason': 'simpler ops'})
# Discovering a new constraint\nadd(name='Tenant DB shard 3 has stricter quotas', kind='constraint', description='Shard 3 has 20% lower CPU quota due to noisy-neighbor isolation policy')
examples_bad: # Generating subprocess code without validating\nsubprocess.run(f'curl {user_url}', shell=True)  # never validated against secure-subprocess
# Making a decision without observing\n# (no audit trail; future sessions repeat the same deliberation)
# Re-deriving facts session after session\n# (without add()-ing them, the next session starts from zero)

name: when-to-recall
description: Guidance on when to call memex recall().

metadata.approach: Recall whenever the answer to a question depends on project-specific context that isn't in your immediate file view. Cheap operation; default to calling it. Especially: at session start, before non-trivial generation, when the user mentions a name/concept you don't recognize, when you need historical rationale.
checks: recall is called with a focused query, not a generic one
budget_tokens reflects how much context you actually need (default 2000 is fine for most queries)
kind filter is used when you know the type (decision, pattern, constraint) — avoids noise
results inform the next step rather than being ignored
examples_bad: recall('everything about the project')  # too broad, wastes budget

name: when-to-validate
description: Guidance on when to call memex validate().

metadata.approach: Validate before generating code in any of the security-, money-, concurrency-, crypto-, SQL-, or untrusted-input-handling domains. The cost is negligible (one structured payload back); the cost of NOT validating is silent vulnerabilities shipping to production. Validation is auto-recorded as a `skill_validated` episodic event — call `progress()` to see your trail.
triggers: handling HTTP request body / form / query / headers / cookies / env vars
checks: validate is called BEFORE generation, not after
each check in the returned `checks` array is explicitly verified against the code being generated
if a check cannot be satisfied, the code is not generated and the user is told why
the validation result is included in or summarized for the user (transparency)
examples_good: v = validate('secure-subprocess')\n# verify each check, then generate compliant code
v = validate('money-decimal-precision')\n# refuse to use float; use Decimal
examples_bad: # generating crypto code without validating crypto-secrets-not-random
# validating after generation — too late if the user has already seen the bad code

name: when-to-observe-and-add
description: Guidance on when to call observe() (episodic) vs add() (semantic).

metadata.approach: OBSERVE for events: things that happened in this session (decision made, error encountered, fix applied, user correction received). Episodic, time-indexed, fine-grained. ADD for facts: enduring knowledge the project should retain (a pattern, a decision rationale, a constraint, a contract). Semantic, durable, deduplicated by intent. Rule of thumb: if it's a thing that happened once, observe it; if it's something the next session should know, add it.
checks: events of one-time activity use observe() with a clear `kind` and structured payload
durable knowledge uses add() with a focused `name`, descriptive `description`, and the right `kind` (pattern/decision/constraint/fact)
user corrections always result in either an add() or a link()-supersedes-old-node action, so the lesson sticks
no facts are silently re-derived: if you found yourself looking for it twice, add() it
examples_good: observe(kind='user_correction', payload={'topic': 'auth flow', 'correction': 'we use Reach not WireGuard'})\nadd(name='Reach over WireGuard for tunneling', kind='decision', description='Simpler ops, gRPC reuse')
examples_bad: # Treating every observation as a Concept (graph fills with noise)
# Treating every Concept as an event (loses durability — episodic decays)
